prompt: The graph below shows the percentage of electricity generated from four sources in the United Kingdom between 1990 and 2020.
model:
The line graph illustrates the proportion of electricity produced from coal, gas, nuclear power and renewable sources in the UK over a thirty-year period starting in 1990.

Overall, the UK's electricity mix changed dramatically. Coal, initially the dominant source, had almost disappeared by 2020, while renewables rose from a negligible share to become the largest single source. Gas also grew considerably, whereas nuclear power remained relatively stable throughout.

In 1990, coal accounted for 65% of electricity generation, far more than nuclear power (21%) and gas, which supplied just 1%. Over the following decade, coal's share fell sharply to 32% in 2000, the same figure as gas, which had expanded rapidly. After a slight rise to 34% in 2005, coal resumed its decline, contributing only 2% by 2020.

Gas was the leading source from 2005, peaking at 45% in 2010 before dropping to 30% five years later and recovering to 36% by the end of the period. Renewables, by contrast, provided a mere 2-4% until 2005, but then surged to 25% in 2015 and 43% in 2020, overtaking gas. Nuclear power fluctuated between 16% and 26%, reaching its highest point in 1995, and finished the period at 16%.
